newsitem.title: BELARUS: Defiant Lukashenko woos Orthodox faithful.
newsitem.headline: Defiant Lukashenko woos Orthodox faithful.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko, defying calls for a political compromise with his foes, wooed Belarussian Orthodox Christians on Thursday ahead of a controversial referendum on increasing his powers.

With three days to go before voting ends on Sunday, Lukashenko told a rally of 10,000 people in the main square of this western border city that it would be "laughable" for him to scrap the referendum.

The 42-year-old president spurned a Russian invitation to peace talks with his opponents on Wednesday, but said he expected Russian prime minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to come to Minsk on a mediation mission on Friday.

"I am not going to share power with anyone," he declared in an interview with Russia's Interfax news agency before returning to the capital Minsk for a meeting with parliament chairman Semyon Sharetsky.

Police stepped in to confiscate red-and-white Belarussian flags -- no longer used under Lukashenko -- waved by a handful of young demonstrators who shouted "impeachment". There was heavy security and some foreign television crews were prevented from filming the rally.

Earlier Lukashenko visited the site of a new Russian Orthodox cathedral under construction on the outskirts of the city, where several hundred believers waited in the rain under umbrellas to greet him.
A priest hailed the president, who strongly favours union with Russia and has proclaimed his conversion from Marxism-Leninism to Orthodoxy, as "Alexander, gatherer of the lands."

"May God help you, dear President Alexander, we will pray for you, you are our protector, the head of our life," the priest said, kissing Lukashenko on both cheeks and addressing him as "Vozhd" (supreme leader).
Lukashenko in reply promised Orthodox Christians freedom of worship and peace, vowing he would not allow a "Smuta" or "Time of Troubles" in Belarus.
The former Soviet republic is mostly Orthodox though it borders Poland and also has Roman Catholic and Eastern-rite Catholic communities.
Lukashenko promised there would be no more demolition of cathedrals as in the Soviet period and said Christianity should be the foundation of Belarussian life.
His trip to Brest was the latest in a series of campaign trips to seek voters' backing against his parliamentary critics.
The real extent of popular support for Lukashenko is hard to test as he has complete control of the media and many critics are afraid to speak out.

Columns of buses from workplaces, organised Soviet-style, brought the crowds to Thursday's rally. However many Belarussians, especially in rural areas, still see the maverick president as a hero and he is widely expected to win the referendum.
